note: Every point carries the eight parts the curriculum requires: a simple explanation, a formula, examples, the mistakes learners actually make, and generator specs for practice, listening, speaking and production. Explanations lead with the patient-teacher version and only then reach for terminology.

points.name: 이에요 / 예요
points.simple: This is Korean's equals sign. You put it after a noun to say something IS that thing. Which of the two you use depends only on whether the noun ends in a consonant — nothing else.
points.technical: The polite non-formal form of the copula 이다. 이에요 after a consonant-final noun, 예요 after a vowel-final one. It attaches directly to the noun with no space.

examples.note: 학생 ends in ㅇ, so 이에요.
의사 ends in a vowel, so 예요.
The single most useful question in the language.

mistakes.why: 학생 ends in a consonant, so it needs the full 이에요.
의사 ends in a vowel. 이에요 after a vowel is a mouthful nobody says.
No space. It glues onto the noun.
이에요 only goes after nouns. 배고프다 is already a verb-like adjective and conjugates on its own.

prompts: Say what you do for a living.

prompts.situation: Someone asks what you do. You are a student.
You point at something on a menu and want to know what it is.

points.name: 은 / 는 (topic)
points.simple: This puts a thing on the table and says 'right, let's talk about this one'. It often carries a quiet comparison: saying 커피는 좋아해요 hints that there is something else you don't like.
points.technical: The topic marker. Marks given information, contrast, or general statements. 은 after a consonant, 는 after a vowel. It replaces 이/가 and 을/를 rather than stacking with them.

examples.note: A general statement about a category.

examples.english: I like coffee but not tea.
examples.note: Two topics held against each other — this is 은/는's speciality.

mistakes.why: The answer to 'who?' is brand-new information, so it takes 이/가. 친구는 would mean 'as for my friend, he came' — answering a question nobody asked.
저 already has 는 attached. 저는 IS 저 + 는.
은/는 replaces 을/를, it does not stack on top of it.

prompts: Say you like one food but not another.

prompts.situation: You want to say that today specifically is busy, unlike usual.

points.name: 이 / 가 (subject)
points.meaning: marks who or what does the action
points.simple: This is your finger pointing straight at who did something. 'THIS one.' Use it when the information is new, or when you are answering the question 'who?' or 'what?'.
points.technical: The subject marker. Marks the grammatical subject, typically carrying new or focused information, and is required inside subordinate clauses where 은/는 cannot appear.

mistakes.why: 저 + 가 contracts to 제가. Likewise 나 + 가 → 내가, 누구 + 가 → 누가.
있다 and 없다 describe existence, not an action done to an object.
좋아하다 is a verb and takes an object. 좋다 is an adjective and takes 이/가 — 김치가 좋아요.

prompts.situation: You look outside and notice it has started raining. Tell your friend.

points.name: 을 / 를 (object)
points.meaning: marks the thing the action happens to
points.simple: This marks what you are doing something TO. Eat what? Read what? Whatever answers that gets 을/를.
points.technical: The accusative marker. In casual speech it is very often dropped when the object is obvious from context.

examples.note: 커피 ends in a vowel → 를.
The 을 is dropped. Extremely common in speech.

mistakes.why: 가다 takes a destination, not an object. The place you go to takes 에.
만나다 takes 을/를 in Korean, even though English says 'meet WITH'.
타다 also takes 을/를. So does 좋아하다.

prompts: Say three things you did today.

prompts.situation: Tell someone you are studying Korean.

points.name: 에 (place / time)
points.simple: An arrow pointing at a place, or a pin stuck in a moment. Where you're going, where something IS, or when something happens.
points.technical: Marks a destination with verbs of motion, a static location with 있다/없다, and a point in time. It does not mark the location of an activity — that is 에서.

mistakes.why: 가다 needs a destination — that is 에.
있다 takes 에, always, with no exceptions.
오늘, 내일, 어제, 지금 and 언제 never take 에. Neither does 매일.

prompts.situation: Someone asks where you are. You're at home.

points.name: 에서 (activity place / from)
points.simple: A little stage the action happens on. If you could film someone doing the verb there, use 에서.
points.technical: Marks the location of a dynamic activity, or a point of origin.

mistakes.why: 공부하다 is an activity, so its location takes 에서.
Both are grammatical but mean opposite things: 한국에 왔어요 is 'I came TO Korea'.

prompts.situation: Tell someone which country you're from.

points.name: 아 / 어요 (present polite)
points.simple: This is the ending you will use more than any other. Take the dictionary form, chop off 다, and add 아요 or 어요 — 아요 if the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, 어요 otherwise. Then a few of them squash together.
points.technical: The polite non-formal declarative. Selection follows vowel harmony; the resulting vowel sequence contracts obligatorily in speech.
points.structure: stem + 아요 (last vowel ㅏ/ㅗ) / 어요 (otherwise); 하다 → 해요

examples.note: ㅓ is not ㅏ or ㅗ, so 어요. Stem ends in a consonant, so no contraction.
Its own special case. Every -하다 verb follows it.

mistakes.why: 가 + 아 must contract. Two identical vowels never sit side by side.
춥다 is ㅂ-irregular: the ㅂ becomes 우 before a vowel.
으-irregular: the ㅡ drops out entirely.
ㄷ-irregular: ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel.

prompts: Say five things you do every day.

prompts.situation: Tell a friend you're drinking coffee right now.

points.name: 았 / 었어요 (past)
points.simple: Make the present-tense form first, then push a ㅆ underneath the last syllable and add 어요. 먹어 becomes 먹었어요. Once you can do the present tense, the past is free.
points.technical: The past marker -았/-었- inserts between stem and ending, selected by the same vowel harmony as the present. Building it from the already-contracted present form avoids re-deriving every irregular.

examples.note: 가 already contracted, so the ㅆ goes straight underneath.

mistakes.why: One past marker is enough.
Contract first, then add ㅆ.
Korean marks past tense on the verb even when the time word already says it.

prompts.situation: A friend asks what you did yesterday. You watched a film.

points.name: 있어요 / 없어요
points.meaning: there is / there isn't; I have / I don't have
points.simple: A box with something in it, or a box with nothing in it. Korean uses the same word for 'there is' and 'I have' — context tells you which.
points.technical: Existential verbs. They take 이/가 on their argument, never 을/를, and 없다 is a separate lexical item rather than a negation of 있다.

mistakes.why: 있다 takes 이/가.
The negative of 있다 is the separate word 없다.
'I am a student' is identity, not existence. That is 이에요.

prompts.situation: You need the toilet in a café. Ask where it is.

points.name: 아니에요
points.simple: The opposite of 이에요. Note that the noun in front takes 이/가, not 은/는.
points.technical: The negative copula 아니다. Its complement is marked with 이/가.

examples.note: Standard modest reply to thanks or a compliment.

mistakes.why: 아니다 takes 이/가.
안 does not negate the copula. 아니다 is its own word.

prompts: Correct a wrong guess about your job.

prompts.situation: Someone assumes you're a teacher. You're not.

points.name: 도 (also)
points.simple: 'Too'. It pushes out 은/는, 이/가 and 을/를 — you never write both.
points.technical: An additive particle that replaces the topic, subject and object markers rather than stacking with them.

mistakes.why: 도 replaces 는.
도 replaces 를.

prompts: Agree that you also like something.

prompts.situation: Your friend says they're a student. So are you.

points.name: 와 / 과, 하고 (and)
points.simple: Three ways to say 'and' between two nouns. 하고 is what people actually say; 와/과 is what they write.
points.technical: 와 after a vowel, 과 after a consonant — note this is the reverse of the usual pattern. 하고 and 랑/이랑 are the colloquial equivalents, 랑 being the most casual.

examples.note: 커피 ends in a vowel → 와. Written register.
빵 ends in a consonant → 과.

mistakes.why: 와/과 run backwards compared to every other particle: 와 after a vowel.
그리고 joins sentences, not nouns.

prompts: Order two things at a café.

prompts.situation: Say you went with a friend.

points.name: 주세요 (please give / please do)
points.meaning: please give me / please do it for me
points.simple: The most useful thing you can learn in your first week. Put it after a noun to ask for the thing, or after a verb's 아/어 form to ask someone to do it.
points.technical: The honorific imperative of 주다. After a noun it requests the item; after the 아/어 form of a verb it requests the action as a favour.
points.structure: noun + 주세요  |  verb 아/어 form + 주세요

mistakes.why: Nothing goes after 주세요. The object particle is usually dropped too.
It attaches to the 아/어 form, so 말하다 → 말해.
Korean verbs go last, always.

prompts.situation: The person is speaking too fast for you. Ask them to slow down.

points.name: 고 싶어요 (want to)
points.simple: Chop 다 off a verb and add 고 싶어요. It only works for what YOU want — talking about what someone else wants needs a different ending.
points.technical: -고 싶다 expresses first-person desire. For a third-person subject Korean requires -고 싶어하다, because inner states of others cannot be asserted directly.

examples.english: I want to go to Korea.
What do you want to eat?

mistakes.why: It attaches to the stem, so 다 comes off first.
You cannot state someone else's inner desire as fact in Korean.
For 'want to be', Korean uses 되다 (become).

prompts.situation: You're hungry and want to tell your friend what you'd like to do.

points.name: 안 and 못 (negation)
points.simple: 안 is a choice — you decided not to. 못 is a wall — something stops you. 'I don't drink' is 안. 'I can't eat spicy food' is 못.
points.technical: 안 is simple negation and cannot combine with adjectives of ability. 못 negates ability or possibility. Both precede the verb; -하다 compounds split around them.
points.structure: 안 / 못 + verb  |  noun + 안/못 + 해요 for -하다 verbs

mistakes.why: -하다 verbs split: the noun comes first, then 안, then 해요.
알다 has no 안 form. Its negative is the separate verb 모르다.
Same idea — 있다's negative is 없다.

prompts.situation: You'd love to come but you have to work.

points.name: -(으)세요 (polite request / honorific)
points.simple: Two jobs in one ending. Said to someone, it's a polite 'please do this'. Said about someone you respect, it raises them. 안녕하세요 is literally this ending on 안녕하다.
points.technical: The honorific marker -(으)시- fused with the polite ending. 으 appears after a consonant-final stem; ㄹ-stems drop their ㄹ. Several common verbs use suppletive honorific stems instead.

examples.note: 자다 → 주무시다, a separate honorific word.

mistakes.why: Never use an honorific about yourself. This is the most common honorific error.
먹다's honorific is the separate verb 드시다, and 께서 replaces 가.
ㄹ-stems drop their ㄹ before ㅅ.

prompts.situation: An older colleague is standing. Offer them a seat.

points.name: -(으)ㄹ까요? (shall we?)
points.meaning: shall we? / shall I? / I wonder
points.simple: Suggests something while leaving the other person room to say no. Much softer than -(으)ㅂ시다, which can sound like an order.
points.technical: Expresses a proposal or conjecture. With a first-person plural subject it proposes; with a third-person subject it wonders aloud.

mistakes.why: -(으)ㅂ시다 sounds bossy directed upward. Use -(으)ㄹ까요? with anyone senior.
가 ends in a vowel, so no 으.

prompts.situation: Suggest getting coffee with a colleague senior to you.

points.name: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (will / going to)
points.simple: Your plan for the future. Note the space — 거 is a real noun meaning 'thing', so this literally reads 'it is a thing that I will do'.
points.technical: The prospective modifier -(으)ㄹ plus the bound noun 것 plus the copula. With a third-person subject it reads as conjecture rather than intention.

examples.english: What are you going to do?

mistakes.why: 거 is a separate noun, so it takes a space.
가 ends in a vowel, so ㄹ attaches directly.
먹 ends in a consonant, so it needs 을.

prompts.situation: Tell someone your plan for the weekend.

points.name: -ㅂ니다 / 습니다 (formal)
points.simple: The formal register. You will hear it constantly from shop staff, on the news and in announcements — and you use it in presentations and interviews. Remember it is always pronounced [슴니다], never [습니다].
points.technical: The deferential style. -ㅂ니다 after a vowel-final stem, -습니다 after a consonant-final one; ㄹ-stems drop their ㄹ. Nasalisation makes the ㅂ surface as [ㅁ].

examples.note: The copula's formal form is 입니다.

mistakes.why: 먹 ends in a consonant.
ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ and take ㅂ니다.
ㅂ before ㄴ becomes ㅁ. This happens every single time.

prompts: Say the same sentence in 해요체 then 합니다체.

prompts.situation: You're introducing yourself at a job interview.

points.name: Native and Sino-Korean numbers
points.simple: Korean has two complete sets of numbers and uses both every day. Count things you can see with 하나 둘 셋. Read numbers off a page — money, dates, minutes, phone numbers — with 일 이 삼.
points.technical: Native numerals combine with counters for objects, people, age and hours. Sino-Korean numerals are used for dates, money, minutes, addresses, floors and numbers above 99. Native 하나/둘/셋/넷/스물 shorten to 한/두/세/네/스무 before a counter.
points.structure: native + counter  |  Sino for written numbers

examples.note: 둘 shortens to 두 before 잔.
Hour is native, minutes are Sino. Both systems in one phrase.

mistakes.why: Before a counter, 둘 becomes 두.
Hours use native numbers, minutes use Sino.
Money is always Sino-Korean.

prompts.situation: Order three coffees.
Say it's half past two.
